title: What a Best-Selling Divorce Memoir Does Not Say About Marriage
gist: Belle Burden's 2026 divorce memoir 'Strangers' has triggered a wave of marital anxiety and pushed readers toward prenups, separate finances and marriage avoidance; this essay argues the correct response is the opposite — a 'union' view of marriage evidenced by shared finances and shared surnames (IFS finds non-surname-sharing couples divorce ~50% more often and ~30% earlier), plus policy levers like covenant marriage and 50-50 custody defaults, against Brad Wilcox's divorce-predicting 'soulmate myth'.

insights.claim: Belle Burden's 'Strangers: A Memoir of Marriage' — the account of a woman whose husband abruptly left their 20-year marriage after an affair, exposing how financially and emotionally vulnerable she had become — is one of 2026's most talked-about books.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A single cultural artefact is measurably shifting attitudes toward marriage risk among women — a demand-side signal for prenups, separate finances and delayed marriage.
insights.locator: It tells the story of a woman whose husband abruptly left

insights.claim: Two of the three dominant readings of the memoir — avoid marriage entirely, or use prenups and financial independence to minimise vulnerability within it — both respond to divorce risk by strengthening individual independence before and within marriage.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Names the emerging default consumer response to divorce risk: legal and financial self-insurance, which sustains demand for family-law and asset-protection services.
insights.locator: Both these readings seek to mitigate the risk of divorce

insights.claim: The author's preferred third reading inverts the logic: avoid divorce by strengthening marriage and de-emphasizing independence, arguing the antidote to a divorce culture is a marriage culture prioritising commitment, unity and family life over individual satisfaction.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The explicit counter-position to the mainstream 'protect yourself' consensus — the fault line on which family policy advocacy will now be fought.
insights.locator: A third view takes the opposite approach

insights.claim: Burden's specific losses were driven by identifiable choices — stepping back from a legal career, financial disengagement from the household, and a risky prenup signed against legal advice — rather than by marriage as such.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The viral lesson drawn from the memoir does not match its own facts; the transmissible risk factors are specific and avoidable, not structural to marriage.
insights.locator: That choice, combined with her financial disengagement

insights.claim: Population-level research shows married women live longer, earn more and report more meaning in their lives than single women, and marriage is strongly associated with higher happiness and greater financial stability for most women.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The base rate contradicts the viral narrative — anecdote-driven sentiment is diverging from the underlying data, a classic setup for mispriced social expectations.
insights.locator: Research shows that marriage is strongly associated with higher happiness

insights.claim: The happiness premium for married mothers relative to single, childless women aged 25-55 is large and growing, meaning married moms are increasingly happier than single women rather than merely happier.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A widening, not narrowing, gap — the well-being divergence between family structures is compounding over time.
insights.quote: Married moms aren’t just happier than single women
insights.locator: for married moms compared to single, childless women

insights.claim: A key measurement caveat: 'unmarried' is not the same as 'never married', so to the extent divorced women sit in the unmarried category, part of the marriage premium may actually be capturing the harms of divorce rather than the absence of marriage.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: An honest methodological concession from a pro-marriage source; it reframes the finding as evidence that divorce is uniquely damaging, which is the author's real argument.
insights.quote: “Unmarried” is not the same as “never married.”
insights.locator: But the story is more complicated than it seems.

insights.claim: The divorce rate more than doubled since the expressive divorce revolution began in the 1960s, which reframed divorce as a form of self-expression and eroded the distinction between good and bad reasons for divorce.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Dates the cultural regime change and its measurable consequence — the baseline against which any pro-marriage policy would be judged.
insights.quote: divorce rate more than doubled since the expressive divorce revolution began in the 1960s
insights.locator: The rise of expressive divorce culture

insights.claim: A Harper's Bazaar report described the memoir as planting widespread paranoia and 'making people hate their husbands', with readers monitoring spouses' phones, scanning for red flags, and one bride-to-be experiencing 24 to 48 hours of sheer panic mid-wedding-planning.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Documents a measurable behavioural contagion from a single book — evidence that marital confidence is fragile and media-sensitive.

insights.claim: This anxiety is a rational response to a genuine structural change: there is no legal protection for marital vows under a no-fault, at-will divorce regime.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Locates the source of marital insecurity in law rather than psychology, which makes it addressable by statute — the basis for the policy proposals that follow.
insights.quote: There is a lack of legal protection for marital vows in a world of no-fault, at-will divorce.

insights.claim: The memoir's author herself hopes her children will 'fall in love with abandon' as she did, an intent directly at odds with the risk-averse conclusions readers are drawing from her book.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The gap between authorial intent and audience takeaway is the actual cultural event here — narratives are being repurposed against their source.
insights.quote: I hope they will fall in love with abandon as I did with their father.

themes.theme: Union View vs. the Soulmate Myth

insights.claim: Couples who share finances generally enjoy longer and more satisfying marriages, with a recent study linking joint bank accounts specifically to better marriages.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A concrete, testable behavioural marker of marital durability — and a datapoint that cuts against the separate-finances advice now spreading online.
insights.locator: Couples who share finances generally enjoy longer

insights.claim: IFS analysis of U.S. divorce rates found that spouses who did not share a surname divorced about 50% more often than those who did, and that divorces among non-sharers occurred roughly 30% earlier in the marriage.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A striking, easily observable proxy variable for divorce risk — surname sharing as a revealed-preference indicator of the union view of marriage.
insights.locator: U.S. divorce rates to compare couples who shared a surname

insights.claim: Brad Wilcox's 'soulmate myth' — the assumption that marriage exists primarily to sustain an intense emotional connection lasting only as long as it remains fulfilling to the self — is associated in his research with higher rates of divorce and conflict.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A named mental model that predicts divorce risk from how spouses conceptualise the marriage, not from their circumstances.
insights.quote: assumes marriage’s primary function is to build and sustain an intense romantic or emotional connection that should last only as long as it remains happy, fulfilling, and lifegiving to the self
insights.locator: This view stands in contrast to what Brad Wilcox

insights.claim: Sharing finances and a surname are treated as expressions of a 'union' view that merges two individuals into a shared identity, project and future — the structural opposite of the independence-maximising strategy.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Converts an abstract philosophical position into two measurable household behaviours, making the thesis empirically checkable.
insights.locator: Sharing finances and a last name expresses a “union” view

insights.claim: At the state level, policymakers can offer 'covenant marriages' — a harder-to-exit marriage contract couples may elect — as a structural response to at-will divorce.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A specific, already-existing legal instrument that could see renewed legislative push if marital-risk anxiety keeps rising.
insights.locator: At the state level, policymakers can consider offering

insights.claim: Some states have addressed the financial incentives to divorce by making 50-50 shared custody the default when couples divorce or separate.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Custody defaults are a lever on divorce economics — a live legislative trend worth tracking across states.
insights.locator: Other states have addressed financial incentives to divorce

insights.claim: The author argues couples should be encouraged to use traditional vows over self-written ones, since traditional vows express unconditional lifelong fidelity while sentimental self-written vows use poetic language to communicate anything but a binding promise.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A cultural-practice recommendation that would be visible in the wedding industry if adopted — a leading indicator of any marriage-culture shift.

insights.claim: The closing argument, invoking C.S. Lewis, is that locking up one's heart to prevent heartbreak produces a heart that is 'unbreakable, impenetrable, irredeemable', so the correct response to divorce risk is embracing dependency rather than retreating into self-sufficiency.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The explicit case against the financial and emotional protectionism now dominant in online relationship advice — the ideological counterweight to the prenup boom.
